cf.title: Fix rescan costing of single-batch hash joins

input.subject: Fix rescan costing of single-batch hash joins

verdict_reasoning: No objection survived at levels 1a, 1b or 2. The problem is stated with two reproducible scripts, and Etsuro Fujita agreed in message #2 that the costing does not match ExecReScanHashJoin(). The confidence is low because the panel raised no objections and the patch code was not read, so the result rests on the prose alone.

brief.title: Fix rescan costing of single-batch hash joins
brief.problem: cost_rescan() charges nothing on rescan for a single-batch hash join, though ExecReScanHashJoin() reruns the outer side and rebuilds the hash table when inner parameters change. A hash join over a LATERAL subquery with sorting or grouping is costed as if that work ran once, so the planner picks slow plans. With plan caching, custom plans also look cheaper than generic plans, so generic plans are never chosen.
brief.proposed_design: On rescan, cost_rescan() charges the outer path's own rescan cost instead of zero. When the inner path is parameterized, it charges the full join cost, because the hash table is rebuilt every loop. The change is in costsize.c only, with a new regression test in join.sql.
author_claims: With 100 groups and a 10k-row table, master picks a hash join at 43-60 ms and the patch picks nested loop plus Memoize at about 1.5 ms.
With a 1M-row lookup table both builds pick the same plan.
The underestimate also appears with GROUP BY, DISTINCT, ORDER BY without LIMIT, and inlined SQL set-returning functions taking an outer column.
Since SQL functions use the plan cache in 18, the underestimate keeps prepared statements and SQL functions on custom plans (19 ms per call versus 0.7 ms generic).
No existing regression plans change; make check, contrib and isolation tests pass; master only.
brief.thread_state: Etsuro Fujita agreed the costing does not match the executor and that the fix is master-only, and plans to review next month. Nazneen Jafri reproduced both scripts on 18.4 builds; no review of the code has been posted.
unclear: The material does not show how the patch costs the parameterized-inner case relative to the outer path's rescan cost, or whether both charges can apply together.
No planning-time or broader benchmark results, such as TPC-H or join-heavy workloads, are reported for plan regressions elsewhere.
The material does not say whether parallel hash joins or multi-batch cases change behavior.
The material does not say whether similar rescan underestimates exist for merge join or other nodes beyond the Aggregate case cited.

touch_points.label: planner behaviour change
touch_points.reason: cost_rescan() in costsize.c charges more for rescans of single-batch hash joins, so nested loop plans over hash joins can change.

touch_points.label: backpatchability
touch_points.reason: The entry is tagged Bugfix, but author and reviewer agree it is master only because it changes plans.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)

questions: When the inner path is parameterized, does the full join cost replace the outer path's rescan cost, or can both charges apply to one join?
Which plans change on a join-heavy benchmark such as TPC-H or the join order benchmark, and do any of them run slower with the patch?
Does the new charge apply to parallel hash joins and to multi-batch hash joins, or do those cases keep their current rescan cost?
How many prepared statements or SQL functions that are fast on custom plans today would move to a slower generic plan with the higher custom plan cost?
Does merge join or another node handled by cost_rescan() have the same underestimate when its input reruns on every rescan?

committability.owner_note: Etsuro Fujita agreed with the diagnosis in message #2 and signed up as reviewer; the owner must know planner costing and the hash join rescan path in the executor.
committability.liability: The owner signs for plan changes in nested loops over hash joins after the next major upgrade, and for reports of queries that become slower, with no backpatch to limit the exposure.
committability.author_follow_up: The author answered the next day and added the CommitFest entry when asked (message #3); no later sign either way in the visible messages.

priority.reason: The patch is 6.2 KB, touches costsize.c and one regression test, and adds no user-visible surface. It affects LATERAL queries and SQL functions on the plan cache in 18, and a planner-area committer plans to review it.

provisional_note: Without the code, nobody checked how the outer rescan charge and the parameterized-inner charge combine, or whether parallel and multi-batch hash joins are affected. The thread reports no plan-change results beyond the regression suite and the two scripts.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Fix unique join costings
precedents_retrieved.summary: Since v10, the planner costs inner_unique joins by treating them as semi joins in compute_semi_anti_join_factors, so join filter costs can drop to zero, as in bug #15383. Two fixes were tried: David Rowley's partial revert of the costing in 9c7f5229ad6, and Tom Lane's stopgap that estimates outer_match_frac as joinrel size over outer rel size, later combined with a per-row cpu_tuple_cost surcharge on non-unique joins.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane rejected the partial revert because it removes the planner's cost preference for inner_unique plans and makes other cases worse. David Rowley found a counterexample to Tom's stopgap. The later combined patch was only a starting point for investigation. Neither author had ideas for a committable fix, which would need the cost model to separate uniqueness quals from filter quals, so the entry was returned after seven commitfests.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: The "stopgap" patch I posted seems unacceptable in view of the counterexample David found, while his original partial-revert patch doesn't look any better than it did then.

precedents_retrieved.title: Hashjoin fall back to block nested hashloop join
precedents_retrieved.authors: Melanie Plageman (melanieplageman), Soumyadeep Chakraborty (soumyadeep2007), Jesse Zhang (essej), David Kimura (dgkimura)
precedents_retrieved.summary: When extreme skew stops repartitioning from bringing a hash join batch under work_mem, the executor falls back to a block nested hash loop for that batch. It loads the inner batch in work_mem-sized stripes, probes the outer batch once per stripe, and tracks outer matches in a bitmap file, for both serial and parallel hash join.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. At the last visible point, the author's June 2020 version had no parallelism on stripes after stripe 0 because the barrier deadlock hazard had no efficient fix, and in September 2020 the CF bot reported a regression test failure.
matched_queries: nested loop inner hash join costing

precedents_retrieved.title: Autovacuum dynamic cost_limit, cost_delay
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch changes autovac_balance_cost() so that a running autovacuum worker's cost limit is capped at a new MAXVACUUMCOSTLIMIT constant (10000) instead of at wi_cost_limit_base. This lets a reload of autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit or autovacuum_vacuum_cost_delay speed up vacuums that are already running.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Masahiko Sawada argued that the cap at wi_cost_limit_base guards against roundoff errors, so raising it to the maximum could set a worker's limit higher than its base value without need. He said the real problem is that wi_cost_limit_base and wi_cost_delay are not updated when the cost is rebalanced, and proposed a different direction that would drop wi_cost_limit_base. The visible messages show no revised patch after his last reply.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I think that the problem here is rather that we
don't update wi_cost_limit_base and wi_cost_delay when rebalancing the
cost.

precedents_retrieved.title: Improve planner cost estimations for alternative subplans
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Melanie Plageman, Tomas Vondra, Tom Lane
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch changes how the planner costs an AlternativeSubPlan (hashed or per-row lookup) for the rest of the query. It replaces the use of the per-row estimate with a heuristic blend of the two alternatives' costs.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewers said that averaging the costs of two alternatives is wrong in principle, because at run time the executor uses one of them. Tomas Vondra expected regressions where the first plan is used, and the author then found queries that ran slower with the patch. The author suggested moving to Tom Lane's approach of passing a number-of-evaluations estimate to cost_qual_eval, or to Andy Fan's proof of concept that picks the SubPlan during planning, and the entry was withdrawn.
matched_queries: generic plan custom plan cost comparison
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I agree that averaging together the costs of the alternatives seems
wrong in principle.  It's going to be one or the other, not some
quantum-mechanical superposition.

precedents_retrieved.title: Better estimate for filter cost
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch changes the per-tuple filter cost of a base relation scan from the sum of all clause costs to a weighted sum. Each clause's cost is weighted by the selectivity of the clauses ordered before it, so expensive clauses such as subplans are costed only for the rows that reach them.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Michael Paquier returned the patch for lack of activity after the July 2018 review, and the author did not respond to it. In that review Ashutosh Bapat doubted the patch helps, because the estimate changes equally for every path of the relation and he could not find a query that would get a better plan. He also asked for an O(n) method in place of repeated clauselist_selectivity() calls, and for the costing to cover joins as well as scans.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: So the accurate estimate doesn't help us to choose one method of scanning the relation over the other method.

precedents_retrieved.title: hash joins with bloom filters
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch builds a Bloom filter over the inner side of a hash join and checks outer tuples against it before the hash table probe or before writing them to a batch file. Filter sizing uses estimated row counts or 1/8 of work_mem, and EXPLAIN ANALYZE reports filter statistics.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author stopped working on it and asked for it to be marked returned with feedback; no one took it over. He said pushing the filter down to the outer scan would make it more useful, but he had no clear plan for that. Robert Haas noted that costing it well enough to avoid regressions looks hard.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I don't expect to work on this anytime soon, so maybe mark it as
returned with feedback instead of moving it to the next CF.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Optimize order of GROUP BY keys".
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Optimize order of GROUP BY keys".
Reverted commit(s): Optimize order of GROUP BY keys
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit db0d67db2401eb6238ccc04c6407a4fd4f985832 and
several follow-on fixes.  The idea of making a cost-based choice
of the order of the sorting columns is not fundamentally unsound,
but it requires cost information and data statistics that we don't
really have.  For example, relying on procost to distinguish the
relative costs of different sort comparators is pretty pointless
so long as most such comparator functions are labeled with cost 1.0.
Moreover, estimating the number of comparisons done by Quicksort
requires more than just an estimate of the number of distinct values
in the input: you also need some idea of the sizes of the larger
groups, if you want an estimate that's good to better than a factor of
three or so.  That's data that's often unknown or not very reliable.
Worse, to arrive at estimates of the number of calls made to the
lower-order-column comparison functions, the code needs to make
estimates of the numbers of distinct values of multiple columns,
which are necessarily even less trustworthy than per-column stats.
Even if all the inputs are perfectly reliable, the cost algorithm
as-implemented cannot offer useful information about how to order
sorting columns beyond the point at which the average group size
is estimated to drop to 1.

Close inspection of the code added by db0d67db2 shows that there
are also multiple small bugs.  These could have been fixed, but
there's not much point if we don't trust the estimates to be
accurate in-principle.

Finally, the changes in cost_sort's behavior made for very large
changes (often a factor of 2 or so) in the cost estimates for all
sorting operations, not only those for multi-column GROUP BY.
That naturally changes plan choices in many situations, and there's
precious little evidence to show that the changes are for the better.
Given the above doubts about whether the new estimates are really
trustworthy, it's hard to summon much confidence that these changes
are better on the average.

Since we're hard up against the release deadline for v15, let's
revert these changes for now.  We can always try again later.

Note: in v15, I left T_PathKeyInfo in place in nodes.h even though
it's unreferenced.  Removing it would be an ABI break, and it seems
a bit late in the release cycle for that.

precedents_retrieved.title: cost_sort improvement
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch reworks cost_sort() so sort cost depends on the number of sort columns, the cost of each comparison function and the column width. It counts comparison calls per column, using estimate_num_groups() to estimate group sizes from the leading columns, and adds empirical multipliers.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author stopped responding after Tomas Vondra asked for the reasoning behind the formulas and questioned the arbitrary constants, such as the 1.5 worst-case multiplier. Later the patch also failed "make check" on join, aggregates and partition_aggregate, and nothing happened before the entry was closed.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I'm sorry, but I'm getting lost in the notation and how you came up with
those formulas - I don't know where to look in the papers, books etc.

precedents_retrieved.title: Support run-time partition pruning for hash join
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch prunes Append subnodes on the outer side of a hash join while the hash table is built: each inner row computes the partitions it can match, and Append skips the others. The design, ported from Greenplum's Partition Selector, builds PartitionPruneInfos in createplan.c, stores pruning results in executor parameters, and can intersect results across several join levels.
precedents_retrieved.objection: David Rowley was concerned that pruning runs for every row put into the hash table, may prune nothing, and has no worst-case overhead figures. The patch's costing therefore chose the pruning hash join only in very conservative cases. He suggested a different first step, parameterized scan paths on the partition key so that parameterized nested loops can use the existing run-time pruning. Richard Guo found this promising, the thread moved to that design, and no new hash join patch appears.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Maybe instead of inventing a very pessimistic part prune Hash Join, it might be better to make the above work without the LATERAL + OFFSET 0 by creating the parameterized paths Seq Scan paths.

precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Improve accounting for memory used by shared hash tables"
Reverted commit(s): Improve accounting for memory used by shared hash tables
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit f5930f9a98ea65d659d41600a138e608988ad122.

This broke the expansion of private hash tables, which reallocates the
directory. But that's impossible when it's allocated together with the
other fields, and dir_realloc() failed with BogusFree. Clearly, this
needs rethinking.

roaster_notes.note: No listed precedent proposed this idea. [P1] and [P4] were planner costing heuristics that failed on counterexamples or averaged alternatives, and this patch aligns cost_rescan() with ExecReScanHashJoin(). Message #1 cites the original cost_rescan() commit and the multi-batch fix, which kept the old assumption, and calls Andrei's Aggregate report related but separate; the thread records no rejection of this idea.

The patch adds no syntax, keyword, GUC, catalog object, psql change or dump format change, so there is no user-facing contract to check against the standard or pg_dump. The only compatibility effect is that some plans change after a major upgrade, which is normal for a master-only costing fix. Whether those plan changes regress other workloads, including more prepared statements moving to generic plans, belongs to the performance angle.

The patch changes only cost estimation in costsize.c plus a regression test. It touches no on-disk format, WAL, catalog, wire protocol or exported struct, so pg_upgrade, standbys and subscribers are unaffected. Plan choices may differ between primary and standby after an upgrade, but that is normal planner behaviour and not persistent state.

The patch changes only planner cost estimates in costsize.c for hash join rescans. It adds no new privilege, object, setting, function or view, and changes no access-control path. A plan choice exposes no data that the user could not already see through EXPLAIN on their own query. No security or privilege objection applies.

From the maintenance and fit angle there is nothing to object to. The patch changes one cost function in costsize.c to match what ExecReScanHashJoin() already does. It adds no new GUC, catalog, API or dependency, and it adds no per-tuple or per-query cost outside planning. It belongs in core, and a committer who knows the planner, Etsuro Fujita, has agreed with the diagnosis and signed up to review it. Two points could not be checked without the code or more data. The material does not show whether the outer rescan charge and the parameterized-inner charge can both apply to one join, and it reports no plan-change results beyond the regression suite. Those belong to the design and performance angles.

The proposal fixes a cost estimate that does not match what ExecReScanHashJoin() does. No existing feature or extension corrects cost_rescan(). Workarounds such as plan_cache_mode = force_generic_plan or enable_hashjoin = off only hide the problem per session or per query, and they do not help the plain-query case in repro_plain.sql.

No demand objection. This fixes planner costing that does not match what ExecReScanHashJoin() does, and it came from a real performance case, which a second person reproduced on 18.4 (message #4). Etsuro Fujita agreed the costing is wrong (message #2). The affected group, LATERAL queries and SQL functions on the plan cache in 18, is broad enough. Plan regressions for other users belong to the design angle.
